# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand is divided into primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, with a national curriculum guiding teaching in state and state-integrated schools. Primary education typically covers Years 1 to 8 (ages 5–13), with secondary education from Years 9 to 13 (ages 13–18). The academic year runs from late January to mid-December. Schools include state (public), state-integrated (former private schools with a "special character"), and private institutions. State schools serve about 85% of students, are government-funded, and governed by elected Boards of Trustees. State-integrated schools levy compulsory attendance dues to maintain private assets. Private schools rely mostly on tuition fees and receive partial government funding.
Māori language education has a rich history beginning with early mission schools teaching in Māori, declining after government policies favored English. From the 1970s through the 1980s, efforts revived Māori-medium education with institutions like kōhanga reo (language immersion preschools) and kura kaupapa Māori (immersion schools). Currently, Māori language education is offered both as a subject in English-medium schools and through immersion schools; enrollment trends show a decline in percentage terms since 2004. The curriculum for all schools covers eight learning areas, with senior students working towards the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA), alongside alternatives like Cambridge International Examinations or the International Baccalaureate. Special needs education is supported by targeted government funding.
Tertiary education is funded through a combination of government subsidies and student fees; students can access loans and allowances to assist with costs. University and other tertiary institutions receive funding based on enrolled student numbers and course demands. Teacher salaries are centrally paid by the Ministry of Education. Despite good funding mechanisms, concerns exist about rising tertiary fees and their impact on participation and skill shortages. Bullying remains an issue in schools, prompting government initiatives to address it.
In summary, New Zealand maintains a predominantly publicly funded, secular education system with increasing recognition and support for Māori language and culture within education, alongside traditional English-medium schooling and modern tertiary education structures.
